name: Omar Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a team of eight claims handlers at the regional office of a big insurance company, on the third floor above a car showroom. I got promoted to team lead eleven months ago, mostly because the last one left and nobody else wanted it. My day is checking the queue at eight, sorting out who takes the messy home-flood claims, signing off payouts under a limit, and sitting in two or three calls with head office. I like my team, honestly, but the spreadsheets they send down from head office wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of being new to managing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Knowing what I don't know. Priya, who's been there nine years, knows the policy wording better than I ever will, and I'm technically her boss. I get paid a bit more than her, not much, and my partner Lina is a nurse on night shifts, so between us we cover rent and not much else. If something big broke, like the car, we'd be on a credit card by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say what everyone says in the kitchen: told you so, it's a fancy autocomplete. Online I'd share something about how the hype money should've gone to the health service. At work I'd just be glad we didn't have to sit through another training day on some new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even the small stuff touches us. A lot of what my team does is routine: checking forms, chasing missing receipts, writing the same letter forty times. If the company shaves even one handler off each team to save a bit, that's one of my eight, and I'd be the one telling them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and try to get better at it, honestly, because I'm still learning. I'd ask my manager, Grace, to put me on the proper team-lead course they keep postponing. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny, but we've never managed to save anything regular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of the usual grind underneath. The rent went up again in spring and Lina's been picking up extra shifts to cover it. So calm about AI, not calm about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the small stuff could cost one handler. Who would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whoever's slowest on the letters, and that's Tom, who's fifty-eight and types with two fingers. Tom (the slowest handler on my team) is the one who stays late to call back old ladies whose kitchens flooded. A spreadsheet won't see that, and I'm not sure I'd be senior enough to argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if head office asked you to pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push back first and ask the union rep, Dev, what our rights are, because we do have a union on site. If it still came down to it, I'd want it done fairly and openly, not quietly. I'd hate it, but I'd rather be in the room than have it done over my head.

say: I'd joke that AI turned out to be **fancy autocomplete**, like most people at work.
I'd say online that the hype money should have gone to **public services** instead.
think: Even small savings could cut **one handler** from my team of eight.
I'm too **junior** to win an argument with head office about who stays.
do: Ask my manager Grace for the **team-lead course** that keeps getting postponed.
Put aside **fifty a month**, the first regular saving my partner and I would have.
Check with the **union rep** what the rules are before any cuts land.
feel: Calm about AI itself but **tired and stretched** by rent and bills.
S0.quote: Tom (the slowest handler on my team) is the one who stays late to call back old ladies whose kitchens flooded.
fieldNote: His worry in the quiet scenario is about **money and rent**, not technology.
He already pictures himself having to **choose who goes**, and dreads it.
The **union** is his first instinct, which matches his politics.

steps.text: Ask Grace (his manager) for the postponed team-lead course this quarter
Set up a fifty-a-month standing order into a savings pot
Ask Dev (the union rep) about team-cut rules before anything happens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to get ahead of it and make sure nobody's thrown under the bus. Online I'd probably post about the company making record profits while cutting claims staff. I'd sound braver online than I'd be in the meeting, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, claims handling is exactly the checking-and-writing work on that card. Head office already trialled a tool that reads car-damage photos and drafts the payout letter. If my team goes from eight to four, they don't need a team lead for four people, so I'm not safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd start using the tools properly instead of now and then, because I'd rather be the one who understands them. I'd get our union to ask for a written plan on retraining, not just a slide deck. And I'd quietly look at jobs in the city an hour away, because there's nothing like this job in our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in my stomach. It's the feeling of watching a queue get shorter every week and knowing what that means. I keep thinking about Lina's face when I tell her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lina that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we might need to move closer to the city, and she'd say her hospital is here. Lina (my partner, a nurse) is the one with the safe job now, which is a strange flip. A year ago I was the one with the career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it came to moving, what gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, because the train to the city is cheaper than the car loan. Then eating out, which is one curry on a Friday. We don't have much fat to trim, that's the problem.

say: I'd say at work that nobody should be **thrown under the bus**.
I'd post online about **record profits** while claims staff get cut.
I'd admit I'm **braver online** than I'd be in the actual meeting.
think: Claims handling is exactly the **checking and writing** the card describes.
A team of four doesn't need a **team lead**, so I'd be at risk too.
do: Start using the claims AI tools **daily** so I understand them first.
Get the **union** to demand a written retraining plan, not slides.
Look quietly at **jobs in the city** an hour away by train.
feel: A knot in the **stomach**, like watching the claims queue shrink each week.
Dread about telling **Lina**, his partner, that they may need to move.
S1.quote: Lina (my partner, a nurse) is the one with the safe job now, which is a strange flip. A year ago I was the one with the career.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that a smaller team makes **his own role** pointless.
His steady streak shows: he'll learn the tools once they're **proven** at work.
The **partner's nursing job** has become the household's anchor.
Moving is real but **blocked** by Lina's hospital job in town.

steps.text: Use the claims photo-reading tool every day for the next three months
Push the union to ask for a written retraining plan
Apply for claims and operations jobs in the city an hour away
Sell the car and switch to the train to clear the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need governments to step in, and fast: a pay floor, retraining, something. At work I'd say it to my team straight, that I don't know more than they do. I wouldn't pretend to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm gone by 2028, and so is most of my floor. Everything I do is screen work: queues, sign-offs, reports, calls. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because nothing I do needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd move every spare penny into savings and stop the Friday curry. I'd look at work where hands matter, like a healthcare assistant job at Lina's hospital, because that gives me three more years before robots. And I'd join every campaign for some kind of basic income, because I don't see another floor for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Honestly, a bit sick. Two years is less time than I've been out of uni with a proper job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the hospital. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. The healthcare assistant pay is lower than mine and the shifts are brutal, I've seen what they do to Lina. But a person still has to lift someone into a bed in 2029, and a claims team lead won't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, the one with nine years in. She's got two kids and a mortgage, and she's brilliant at something that won't be needed. I'd worry I'd be the one reading her the redundancy script, then reading my own.

say: I'd say governments must act **fast**, with a pay floor and retraining.
I'd tell my team plainly that I **don't have a plan** either.
think: My job and most of my floor are **gone by 2028**.
Robots arriving **three years later** doesn't help, because my work is all screen work.
do: Move every spare penny into **savings** and drop the Friday takeaway.
Apply to be a **healthcare assistant** at the hospital where Lina works.
Join campaigns for a **basic income** as the only realistic floor.
feel: Alarmed and **a bit sick** at how short two years is.
S2.quote: A person still has to lift someone into a bed in 2029, and a claims team lead won't exist.
fieldNote: He grasps the **thinking-first, robots-later** order and uses it to plan a switch.
The **hospital job** is a pay cut he'd take to buy three years.
His politics turn into concrete support for a **basic income**.

steps.text: Stop takeaways and move every spare pound into savings
Apply for healthcare assistant shifts at Lina's (his partner's) hospital
Sign up with a basic-income campaign and go to meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd push the company to say it openly. At the union meeting I'd ask for a proper transition fund. Online I'd be less angry and more practical, sharing what retraining is actually out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's still the same end for my job, just later. But five years means I could finish something real, not panic into the first thing. The thinking part of claims goes in 2031, and I'd want to be out of it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a part-time course, maybe the two-year nursing associate route, since Lina could coach me through it. I'd keep the team-lead job while I study, because we need the pay. And I'd ask the union to get the company to fund the course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan to hold on to. Five years of warning is like a long notice period instead of being marched out. I'd still lie awake some nights, but less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you were braver online than in meetings. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit. With five years there's time to organise rather than just react. I think I'd actually stand up at the union meeting, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the money while you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets very tight. We'd skip a holiday for three years and Lina would keep the extra shifts, which I feel bad about. I'd probably ask my mum for help with course books, which I hate asking.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so the company should be open about it.
I'd ask at the union meeting for a **transition fund** for staff.
think: My job still **ends**, but around 2031 instead of 2028.
Five years is long enough to **finish real training**, not grab the first thing.
do: Start a **part-time nursing associate** course in the first year.
Keep the **team-lead pay** while studying, because the household needs it.
Ask the union to get the company to **fund course fees**.
feel: Anxious, but steadier, like a **long notice period** rather than being marched out.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is like a long notice period instead of being marched out. I'd still lie awake some nights, but less.
fieldNote: The extra time turns panic into a **study plan** he can follow.
He'd finally **speak up** at the union, which he admits he's avoided.
Money stays the bind: **Lina's extra shifts** carry the cost of his training.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time nursing associate course next September
Ask the union to make the company pay course fees
Ask his mum to help with the cost of course books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and the worst thing would be to waste it pretending it isn't coming. At work I'd want every team lead to have a plan for their people. Online I'd probably share it as a reason to fund adult education properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd be thirty-seven when the claims work goes. That's young enough to have a second career, which honestly feels okay. My bigger worry is whether we can afford to have kids on these wages in the middle of all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in claims for now and get properly good at it, and use the AI tools as they arrive. In a couple of years I'd start the nursing associate course, once we've built a small cushion. And I'd be at the union meetings pushing for retraining money to be part of every pay deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. There's room to breathe. It's the rent and the idea of kids that keeps me up more than the robots, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might push it later. Lina wants kids before thirty-two, and I don't want to start a family the year my job disappears. So we'd probably plan around the nursing course rather than around the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you stay in management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if managing turns into looking after people rather than spreadsheets. But I'm not the best at the spreadsheet side anyway, so if that goes, fine. I'd rather bet on something with people in the room.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift we shouldn't waste pretending.
I'd argue online for proper funding of **adult education**.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when claims work goes, young enough for a second career.
Whether we can afford **kids** on these wages worries me more than AI.
do: Stay in claims, get better at it and use **AI tools** as they arrive.
Start the **nursing associate** course in about two years, after building a cushion.
Push the union to put **retraining money** into every pay deal.
feel: Uneasy rather than scared, with **room to breathe**.
Still kept awake by **rent and kids** more than by robots.
S4.quote: I don't want to start a family the year my job disappears. So we'd probably plan around the nursing course rather than around the robots.
fieldNote: With ten years his worries shift back to **rent** and **starting a family**.
He'd use the time to **save first**, then retrain, a careful sequence.
He doesn't feel attached to **management** itself, only to working with people.

steps.text: Use each new claims AI tool as head office rolls it out
Build a three-month cushion before starting any course
Push the union to add retraining money to pay talks
Plan children around finishing the nursing course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question, because there's no time to train for anything and we've got no savings to cover the gap. What would help is paid retraining, real money while you study, not a voucher for an online course. And something like a basic income so people like Lina aren't carrying everyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to manage people when you're scared yourself. Nobody trains you for telling Priya (a colleague with nine years in) that her job's at risk when yours is too. I think a lot of new team leads are going to be in that spot.

headlineQuote: Nobody trains you for telling Priya (a colleague with nine years in) that her job's at risk when yours is too.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old claims team lead**, eleven months into managing eight people at a regional insurance office.
He and his partner Lina, a **night-shift nurse**, cover rent with almost nothing saved.
He leans **left and pro-union**, and his first instinct in every scenario is to organise.
He sees his screen-based job as **directly in line** for AI, and plans a move toward hospital work.
More time steadily calms him, until **rent** and **starting a family** worry him more than AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to retrain and no savings to cover the gap.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with real income while studying, not a voucher for an online course.
A **basic income** so his partner isn't carrying the whole household.
